---
title: "`tr`: Translate"
---

`tr` (short for **translate**) is a Unix filter that transforms characters in its input stream — one character at a time — and writes the result to stdout. It doesn't work on lines or fields like `sed`/`awk`; it works on a pure character-by-character basis.

## Basic shape

```
tr [OPTIONS] SET1 [SET2]
```

- It reads from **stdin only** (no filename argument — you must pipe or redirect input in).
- **SET1** and **SET2** are lists of characters, expressed as literal characters, ranges (`a-z`), or POSIX classes (`[:upper:]`, `[:digit:]`, etc).

```
        stdin            tr SET1 SET2           stdout
  ──────────────►    ┌───────────────────┐   ──────────────►
   "Hello"           │ each char in SET1 │      "Uryyb"
                     │ mapped to same    │
                     │ position in SET2  │
                     └───────────────────┘
```

## Core uses

**1. Translate (replace) characters — the default mode**

Each character in SET1 is replaced by the character at the same position in SET2.

```bash
echo "Hello World" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'
# HELLO WORLD

echo "hello" | tr 'el' 'ip'
# hippo   (e→i, l→p)
```

**2. Delete characters — `-d`**

Removes every character found in SET1. No SET2 needed.

```bash
echo "h3ll0 w0rld" | tr -d '0-9'
# hll wrld
```

**3. Squeeze repeats — `-s`**

Collapses consecutive runs of a repeated character into a single instance.

```bash
echo "aaabbbccc" | tr -s 'a-c'
# abc

echo "too    many   spaces" | tr -s ' '
# too many spaces
```

**4. Complement — `-c`**

Inverts SET1 to mean "everything *not* in this set."

```bash
echo "hello123world" | tr -cd '0-9'
# 123     (keep only digits, delete everything else)
```

## Everyday one-liners

```bash
# Convert Windows line endings to Unix
tr -d '\r' < win.txt > unix.txt

# Count words (translate spaces to newlines, then count lines)
echo "one two three" | tr ' ' '\n' | wc -l

# Strip non-printable / control characters
cat file | tr -cd '[:print:]\n'

# ROT13 (classic party trick)
echo "hello" | tr 'a-zA-Z' 'n-za-mN-ZA-M'
```

## On zsh vs bash

`tr` itself is an external binary (`/usr/bin/tr`), not a shell builtin — so it behaves **identically in zsh and bash**. macOS ships the BSD version of `tr`, which has slightly different flag support than GNU `tr` (e.g. no `--help`, and character-class syntax can be pickier). If you `brew install coreutils`, you'd get GNU `tr` as `gtr`, which is a bit more forgiving with things like Unicode ranges.
